name: Orangism
summary: Orangism in the Kingdom of the Netherlands is attachment to the House of Orange as the country's royal dynasty. After the Orange monarchy was founded in 1813 it tied the flag, anthem, constitution and national feeling to the dynasty, and from the later nineteenth century liberal politicians, commerce and the royal house promoted it to hold together a nation divided by religion and class. It presents the monarch as a symbol above the parties and of national unity, and in its popular form it set loyal subjects against the anti-monarchist socialists.
scope: Orangism in the Kingdom of the Netherlands from the founding of the Orange monarchy in 1813, chiefly the official and popular Orangism of the nineteenth century that te Velde and Petterson describe as liberal-stimulated attachment to the House of Orange used for nation building (s3, s8, s9), with the monarch reduced to a unifying symbol after 1848 (s10). It excludes the oppositional pro-stadholder Orangism of the Dutch Republic (a separate entry, distinguished by s11), Belgian and Luxembourg Orangism, the Irish Orange Order, and the twentieth-century use of orange by Flemish nationalists (s10). The 1814 constitution and the views of individual monarchs (Wilhelmina's own notes) are not treated as Orangism's own texts.

notes: Later pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-12) under rules 5. The first pass rested almost entirely on Wikipedia and on inferences from Orangism's liberal character; every such answer is nulled with its history kept, and the answers now rest only on the scholarship that defines the term. Themes searched: government (monarchy, succession, head of state, parliament, democracy: te Velde 2010 ch. on the monarchy), society (class, nation, religion, socialists: te Velde and Petterson 2013, Petterson 2017, Beyen), culture (heritage, continuity), world (Belgian secession, colonies, Boer War support), economy, liberty, ecology, technology. Economy, world, liberty, ecology and technology hold no Orangist position in these sources: Orangism is attachment to a dynasty and a national symbol, not a programme. Popular violence against socialists (Oranjefurie 1887) is adherents' conduct, not a stated position, and is not used. Sources not reached: te Velde, Gemeenschapszin en plichtsbesef (1992) and his chapter in Denes (ed.), Liberty and the Search for Identity (2006) are not openly available; the full Memoria e Ricerca article is paywalled (abstract only); te Velde's 'Cannadine, twenty years on' in Mystifying the Monarch (OAPEN) is behind a bot check (Anubis) and was not retried; Van Eijnatten, 'Oranje en Nederland zijn een' (De negentiende eeuw 23, 1999) has no online copy found. The protestant 'God, Nederland en Oranje' strand and the liberal cross-confessional strand point different ways on religion, which is left null.
